transcript:
Meeting Header
Date: 2025-05-09
Time: 11:00 AM PT
Duration: 47 min
Title: AWS Marketplace private offer process (regulated workloads ABM + co-sell alignment)
Attendees (Redwood): Ben Carter, Soojin Lee, Tyler Benson, Michael Grant
Attendees (AWS): Megan Sullivan, Rahul Iyer, Nicole Chen

Summary (auto)
- Walked through the end-to-end AWS Marketplace private offer workflow and common gotchas (buyer account, legal entity, start/end dates, EULA vs CPPO, support terms).
- Aligned on what claims are safe for regulated workloads and how to position Redwood Dedicated vs Private in AWS conversations.
- Discussed how to tag ABM accounts for AWS co-sell (ACE) and what information AWS needs to engage field teams.
- Confirmed next steps: AWS checklist, Redwood target list + messaging snippets, and follow-up working session.

Topics (auto)
1) Private offer setup steps + timeline
2) Compliance positioning + evidence pack sequence
3) Co-sell / ACE registration and account alignment
4) Attribution and measurement for partner-influenced pipeline

Questions (auto)
- What info does AWS need to start a co-sell motion for a target account?
- When should Redwood choose Marketplace private offer vs direct contract?
- What compliance language is acceptable in Marketplace listing / offer notes?

00:00 Ben Carter: Cool. Thanks everyone for joining. This is Ben from Redwood, I run growth / ABM for this pilot. We wanted to do a practical walkthrough on the Marketplace private offer flow and then how we should line that up with the regulated vertical ABM we’re kicking off.

00:15 Megan Sullivan: Yep, sounds good. I’m Megan, I’m on the AWS Marketplace ISV GTM side. Rahul’s our PSA and Nicole’s on ACE operations.

00:24 Rahul Iyer: Hey everyone.

00:25 Nicole Chen: Hi. Nice to meet you all.

00:28 Ben Carter: Great. Quick intros on our side—Soojin is product marketing, Tyler is marketing ops and attribution, Michael is legal.

00:36 Soojin Lee: Hi.

00:38 Michael Grant: Hello.

00:40 Tyler Benson: Hey.

00:43 Ben Carter: Megan, do you want to start with like, the canonical steps? We keep hearing “it’s easy” and then in reality there’s five systems.

00:52 Megan Sullivan: (laughs) That’s fair. I’ll do the high-level, then Nicole can do the step-by-step. Basically: you have your Marketplace product already listed, and then for a specific customer you create a private offer. That can be either a custom price, custom terms, or both, depending on how your listing is set up.

01:10 Ben Carter: Right. And we’re mostly talking about enterprise regulated customers—finserv and healthcare—so they often want a paper trail.

01:18 Megan Sullivan: Exactly. In those cases, private offer is common because procurement can route through AWS as the seller-of-record, and some customers prefer that. Timeline depends on how quickly the buyer accepts and whether they also require a separate DPA or security addendum.

01:34 Michael Grant: And that’s one of our questions. If the transaction is through AWS, do we still end up negotiating our own DPA?

01:42 Megan Sullivan: It depends. I’ll let Rahul and Nicole answer but generally: the Marketplace terms cover certain things, but many enterprise buyers still want a direct DPA with the ISV, especially if there’s any data processing. Even if it’s “through Marketplace,” you can attach additional terms in the private offer, or point to your standard DPA.

02:01 Rahul Iyer: Yeah, and for regulated workloads, security folks might request your SOC 2 report, retention policy, that kind of stuff. Marketplace doesn’t replace those. Think of it more as procurement channel and billing.

02:16 Ben Carter: Got it. Nicole, can you do the “if I’m sitting in the console today, what do I click” version?

02:21 Nicole Chen: Sure. So, prerequisites: you need to be onboarded to Marketplace management portal, your product has to be public or at least limited-availability, and you need to have permissions to create offers.

02:34 Nicole Chen: Workflow is: Marketplace Management Portal → Offers → Create Offer → Private Offer. You’ll select the product, then enter the buyer’s AWS account ID. Common issue is people only have the company name, but you need the 12-digit account ID.

02:52 Tyler Benson: So we need to ask for account ID early, basically.

02:55 Nicole Chen: Yes. Then you define pricing dimensions (for SaaS it might be per token, per seat, usage-based, etc.) and then term length, start date, end date. You can include EULA changes if your listing allows it; otherwise you attach “custom terms” as an addendum.

03:15 Michael Grant: When you say attach, do you mean a PDF in the offer?

03:19 Nicole Chen: It’s usually a URL reference or text field, depending on your configuration. Some sellers attach a document. I’ll send you the checklist.

03:27 Ben Carter: For Redwood, we have hosted API but also dedicated capacity and private deployments. Is Marketplace compatible with private deployment licensing?

03:38 Megan Sullivan: Yes, but you want to be clear on the product type. Some companies do “SaaS contract” for the platform fee and then handle infra separately. If it’s deployed in the customer’s VPC, you can still transact the license/support through Marketplace.

03:56 Rahul Iyer: And you can align it to their AWS spend if they have an EDP—enterprise discount program—sometimes they want things in Marketplace because it counts toward commit.

04:06 Ben Carter: That’s super relevant. Our ABM targets tend to be AWS-heavy, especially in finserv.

04:13 Soojin Lee: On the compliance side, we’re trying to keep language tight. We’ve had internal debate about “HIPAA-ready” versus “supports HIPAA-aligned controls.” What’s AWS’ expectation for claims in co-sell notes?

04:29 Megan Sullivan: Great question. In general, avoid definitive certification language unless you have it. For HIPAA, AWS will be cautious. Better is: “supports deployment in customer-controlled VPC, encryption in transit/at rest, audit logs, and can sign a BAA where applicable” — but only if true and reviewed by legal.

04:47 Michael Grant: On BAA specifically—if we don’t have a standard BAA motion yet, we should not imply it.

04:52 Soojin Lee: Exactly.

04:54 Megan Sullivan: Then don’t mention BAA. Keep it to factual controls.

05:00 Rahul Iyer: Also data residency. If you can pin region or do on-prem, say that as an option. Don’t say “data never leaves” unless you can prove it end-to-end.

05:12 Ben Carter: Okay. So if we have regulated landing page copy that says “VPC and on-prem options,” that’s okay.

05:18 Megan Sullivan: Yep.

05:19 Tyler Benson: For measurement, we’re planning UTMs and tracking partner influence. If AWS sends traffic to our regulated landing page, can we get attribution back through ACE as well?

05:30 Nicole Chen: ACE will track the co-sell opportunity and partner-sourced or partner-influenced status, but it’s not a web analytics tool. What I recommend is: use UTM parameters for your side, and for AWS side, make sure the opportunity is registered in ACE and mapped to the right account and contact.

05:49 Tyler Benson: Makes sense.

05:50 Ben Carter: Let’s talk about co-sell alignment with ABM. We have a target list of accounts. What’s the best way to get AWS field engaged without spamming them with like 80 names?

06:04 Megan Sullivan: Start with a smaller set—top 20 to 30—where you have intent signals. Then in ACE, you can create co-sell opportunities or at least tag accounts you’re working. Rahul can help route to the correct account teams.

06:21 Nicole Chen: Minimum data for ACE: customer name, AWS account ID if you have it, stage (like discovery, POC, procurement), expected close date, and what you want AWS to do (intro, exec alignment, procurement guidance).

06:38 Ben Carter: Great. We can do that. Our ABM success metrics are meetings, SQLs, and pilots/POCs. So we’d probably register once we have a meeting or at least active conversation.

06:51 Megan Sullivan: That’s the right threshold.

06:53 Soojin Lee: In terms of messaging for AWS field, what resonates with regulated buyers from your perspective? Is it more “security and compliance” or “performance economics”?

07:05 Rahul Iyer: Both, but sequence matters. For CISO/security folks: audit logs, encryption, SSO, retention controls. For platform/ML: predictable throughput, latency, cost. In regulated environments, they won’t even look at performance until the security box is plausible.

07:23 Ben Carter: That mirrors what we’re seeing.

07:25 Megan Sullivan: And the big differentiator you have is deployment flexibility: hosted, dedicated, VPC/on-prem. That’s easy for our field to understand.

07:36 Ben Carter: Yep.

07:38 Michael Grant: I have a legal/process question. In Marketplace private offer, are we allowed to reference our own SLA terms? Or do they have to be AWS standard terms?

07:49 Nicole Chen: You can reference your SLA as part of the offer terms, but it has to be consistent with your listing and not conflict with AWS terms. Many sellers include an SLA attachment or a URL.

08:04 Michael Grant: And if a customer wants a negotiated SLA, we’d incorporate that via the private offer custom terms.

08:10 Nicole Chen: Correct.

08:12 Ben Carter: And timeline wise—if we have a customer in procurement, what’s the realistic time from “we want a private offer” to “they can click accept”?

08:23 Megan Sullivan: If you have buyer account ID and your terms are standard, you can create the private offer in a day. The gating factor is the buyer’s internal approvals. Some banks take weeks.

08:36 Ben Carter: (laughs) Yeah.

08:38 Rahul Iyer: Also, the buyer has to accept it in their console. Sometimes the person you’re talking to can’t accept because they don’t have permissions.

08:47 Ben Carter: So we need to ask: who is the Marketplace buyer, who can accept offers.

08:52 Nicole Chen: Exactly.

08:54 Soojin Lee: One more compliance positioning question. For regulated workloads, we have a “security evidence pack” index with SOC 2 process, audit log samples, encryption diagrams. Can we share that through AWS channels? Or do you need it redacted/hosted somewhere specific?

09:12 Megan Sullivan: You can share it, but be mindful of confidentiality. Usually you provide it directly to the customer under NDA. For AWS field, you can share the index and say “available under NDA.” Don’t blast the SOC report to a broad distro.

09:29 Michael Grant: Yeah, our SOC 2 report is under NDA.

09:32 Ben Carter: That’s consistent with our internal policy.

09:35 Tyler Benson: For co-sell notes, do we put “SOC 2 Type II available under NDA” and link to the request path?

09:42 Megan Sullivan: That’s fine.

09:44 Nicole Chen: Yep.

09:46 Ben Carter: Can we switch to private offer specifics around pricing? Our products are usage-based in some cases. Does Marketplace support metered billing like tokens?

09:57 Megan Sullivan: Marketplace has usage-based dimensions, but you’ll want to map it cleanly. Many AI vendors simplify to a few dimensions rather than per-token exactly. But you can do “units” that correspond to tokens, as long as it’s consistent.

10:13 Tyler Benson: And that impacts how we report internally.

10:16 Megan Sullivan: Right.

10:17 Ben Carter: For the ABM pilot, we’re likely doing pilots with credits. How does that work in Marketplace? Like can we do a $0 private offer?

10:28 Nicole Chen: You can do discounted offers, including 100% discount for a period, but check your internal constraints and AWS rules. A lot of vendors do a short-term $0 or very low-cost offer for evaluation, then a paid renewal.

10:44 Michael Grant: From legal side, we’d want to ensure evaluation terms are clear. If it’s $0 but includes support and access, you still have risk.

10:53 Ben Carter: Understood.

10:55 Rahul Iyer: Also on regulated accounts, sometimes they don’t want “free” because procurement flags it. A small paid amount through Marketplace can actually be easier.

11:06 Ben Carter: That’s a good tip.

11:08 Soojin Lee: In terms of positioning Dedicated vs Private when routed through AWS: do you see confusion? Like “private offer” sounds like “private deployment.”

11:19 Megan Sullivan: Yes, that happens. You’ll want to clarify language: “AWS Marketplace private offer” is a commercial construct, not necessarily a deployment model.

11:29 Ben Carter: Great point.

11:31 Nicole Chen: I’ve seen sellers literally rename in emails: “Marketplace private offer (commercial)” so the customer doesn’t assume it’s VPC.

11:40 Ben Carter: We’ll do that.

11:42 Rahul Iyer: And from architecture: if you’re doing VPC deployment, align with AWS reference patterns. Mention CloudWatch logs, KMS integration, VPC endpoints, that kind of stuff.

11:55 Ben Carter: Yep. Our SE team has diagrams.

11:58 Soojin Lee: One more question on compliance wording. Our landing page CTA is either “book a security review” or “download benchmark.” From AWS perspective, what works better to drive co-sell engagement?

12:11 Megan Sullivan: For regulated buyers, “security review” is strong, but it can feel heavy. A benchmark download might get more top-of-funnel, but then you need follow-up. I’d do both: benchmark as a lightweight asset, and a secondary CTA for security review.

12:28 Tyler Benson: We can structure it that way.

12:30 Ben Carter: On our side, we’re trying to build pipeline for Dedicated and Private. So we want meetings.

12:36 Megan Sullivan: Then optimize for meeting CTA.

12:39 Ben Carter: Cool.

12:40 Nicole Chen: Also: when you do co-sell, AWS field likes a crisp ask. Like “We need intro to security leader” or “We need help navigating Marketplace procurement.” Not “please help.”

12:51 Ben Carter: Makes sense.

12:53 Ben Carter: Let’s talk about what we should send you after this. We have an ABM target list for finserv and healthcare. We can mark which ones are AWS-first and which are multi-cloud. Is that useful?

13:05 Rahul Iyer: Very.

13:06 Megan Sullivan: Yes.

13:07 Nicole Chen: And if you can include region (NA/EMEA) and whether there’s an existing AWS account team relationship, even better.

13:16 Ben Carter: We can do that.

13:18 Michael Grant: And for private offer creation, do you have a template of the fields we need to collect from the buyer upfront? Like legal name, address, etc.

13:30 Nicole Chen: Yes. Buyer AWS account ID, legal entity name, and who will accept. Sometimes they need a PO number internally, but that’s on them.

13:41 Michael Grant: Great.

13:43 Ben Carter: Can we ask about the “seller-of-record” question? Some of our buyers want Redwood as vendor, not AWS. Is that a blocker for Marketplace?

13:55 Megan Sullivan: It’s just preference. If they require direct vendor onboarding, then you might do direct contract. Marketplace is often easier for accounts with AWS procurement already in place. You can offer both and let customer choose.

14:12 Ben Carter: That aligns with our approach.

14:15 Soojin Lee: For AWS co-sell, can we still co-sell if the deal is not through Marketplace? Like direct contract.

14:22 Megan Sullivan: Yes, co-sell isn’t contingent on Marketplace. ACE is about joint selling on AWS, regardless of transaction channel.

14:32 Ben Carter: Okay. That’s important.

14:34 Tyler Benson: For reporting, we’re going to define partner-influenced pipeline. Is “ACE registered” the cleanest marker on your side?

14:43 Nicole Chen: It’s one marker. There’s also partner-sourced vs partner-influenced fields. But yes, ACE registration helps.

14:53 Ben Carter: Great.

15:00 (crosstalk)

15:02 Ben Carter: Sorry, go ahead Rahul.

15:04 Rahul Iyer: Just adding: for regulated workloads, AWS field may ask about your encryption model—KMS integration, customer-managed keys. If you have documentation, include a short bullet in the co-sell description.

15:18 Soojin Lee: We do, but we have to be careful on exact wording. We support KMS integration in Private deployments; hosted is different.

15:27 Rahul Iyer: Exactly—be precise.

15:30 Ben Carter: Okay. Maybe we’ll create a small “what’s true per deployment mode” snippet for partner field.

15:37 Megan Sullivan: That would be great.

15:39 Ben Carter: Nicole, any other common gotchas on private offers?

15:44 Nicole Chen: Three gotchas: (1) wrong AWS account ID; offer goes nowhere. (2) start date in the past or too soon; buyer can’t accept. (3) terms mismatch with listing; the offer fails review. Also, if you’re doing multi-year, define renewal terms clearly.

16:02 Michael Grant: Is there an AWS review step? Like does AWS approve the private offer?

16:07 Nicole Chen: Not always, but there can be validation. If you’re changing EULA, it may trigger review.

16:15 Michael Grant: Understood.

16:17 Ben Carter: For regulated customers, we also have to manage security questionnaires quickly. Does AWS have a standardized security artifact exchange or is it all bespoke?

16:28 Rahul Iyer: It’s mostly bespoke. Some customers use AWS Artifact for AWS docs, but for ISVs they’ll send you their questionnaire.

16:38 Ben Carter: Yep.

16:40 Soojin Lee: For healthcare, we’re careful not to over-claim “HIPAA.” AWS field sometimes says “HIPAA eligible services.” That doesn’t apply to us.

16:50 Megan Sullivan: Correct. Don’t use “HIPAA eligible” unless you’re an AWS service. Use “supports HIPAA-aligned controls” only if legal signs off.

17:02 Michael Grant: And even that we should say “can support deployments in customer-controlled environments that meet their compliance obligations.”

17:11 Soojin Lee: Yes.

17:13 Ben Carter: Cool. Let’s talk about a concrete workflow for ABM + co-sell. Our plan: we run outbound sequences; when someone responds and we book a meeting, we decide if it’s co-sell eligible, then we register in ACE. That sound right?

17:28 Megan Sullivan: Yep.

17:29 Nicole Chen: And in the ACE registration, put a clear ask. If you want an intro to account team, say that.

17:35 Ben Carter: Okay.

17:37 Tyler Benson: Can we add a step where we pre-tag the top accounts to Rahul for account team mapping even before a meeting? Like “heads up” list.

17:48 Rahul Iyer: You can, but keep it small and high-confidence. Otherwise it becomes noise.

17:54 Ben Carter: We’ll do top 20.

17:56 Soojin Lee: For finserv, we’re targeting platform engineering + security. Can AWS help with connecting to security leadership? Or is it mostly IT?

18:07 Megan Sullivan: Depends on account. Often AWS has relationships with infra/security leadership, but it’s not guaranteed. If you give us the contact you’re aiming for, we can see.

18:18 Ben Carter: Great.

18:20 Michael Grant: Switching back to commercial: If a customer wants a liability cap change, can that go into private offer terms? Or do they force direct contract?

18:32 Megan Sullivan: You can put custom terms, but for heavy negotiations, some customers prefer direct. Marketplace isn’t meant to be a full redline platform.

18:42 Michael Grant: That’s what I assumed.

18:45 Ben Carter: Okay.

18:46 Nicole Chen: Also, for some customers, Marketplace private offers are easier if they accept your standard terms. If they need big changes, they’ll still require direct negotiation.

18:56 Ben Carter: Understood.

19:00 Ben Carter: Any best practices for describing product in the private offer notes? Like what gets pasted into the offer description.

19:09 Nicole Chen: Keep it simple: product name, term, price, what’s included (support tier), and any usage limits. Avoid heavy marketing copy. It’s a procurement document.

19:22 Soojin Lee: Good call.

19:24 Tyler Benson: And no risky claims.

19:26 Nicole Chen: Exactly.

19:28 Ben Carter: We’ve been asked about “audit logs” a lot. Can we mention audit logs as a feature and include sample schema as part of evidence pack?

19:38 Rahul Iyer: Yes. That helps. In regulated accounts, audit trail is huge.

19:45 Megan Sullivan: Just be careful: don’t say “meets all regulatory requirements.” Say “provides audit logs with fields X, Y, Z” and “exports to customer SIEM” if true.

19:56 Ben Carter: Okay.

20:00 Ben Carter: We’re at about 20 minutes. Anything else we should cover? Maybe the follow-up working session—what should we do there?

20:08 Nicole Chen: In the working session, we can walk through creating a test offer in a sandbox, if you have one, and confirm permissions and where you’d attach terms.

20:18 Michael Grant: That would be useful.

20:20 Tyler Benson: And I can align attribution tracking plus lead source mapping.

20:25 Megan Sullivan: Great.

20:27 Ben Carter: Perfect. Before we close, let’s recap action items.

20:32 Ben Carter: Nicole, you’ll send the private offer checklist and minimum info required.

20:36 Nicole Chen: Yes, by Monday.

20:38 Ben Carter: We’ll send the target account list—top 30—with regions and which are good co-sell candidates.

20:44 Ben Carter: Soojin will send approved regulated messaging snippets for AWS field, especially around what we can and cannot say about HIPAA, residency, etc.

20:53 Soojin Lee: Yep.

20:54 Ben Carter: Tyler will share UTM convention and what we’d like from AWS in terms of referral links.

21:00 Tyler Benson: Yep.

21:02 Ben Carter: Michael will review the Marketplace flow from a legal perspective, where we can reference SLA/DPA, and what should stay out of the offer.

21:10 Michael Grant: Yes.

21:12 Ben Carter: Then we schedule a 30 minute working session next week.

21:16 Megan Sullivan: Sounds good.

21:18 Ben Carter: Awesome. Thanks all.

21:21 Megan Sullivan: Thanks.

21:22 Rahul Iyer: Thank you.

21:23 Nicole Chen: Thanks everyone.

(Transcript ends — Fireflies capture cut off a few minutes early; meeting likely ended shortly after recap.)
